request: hi, I'm HL and for my HL essay I'm thinking of comparing how two newspapers reported the same protest. My teacher keeps saying that the passive voice and "nominalisation" in headlines are "ideological" and that a linguist basically proved this using British newspaper headlines in the 1970s, but she couldn't remember the details when I asked. Can you explain properly: (1) what an agentless passive and a nominalisation actually do to a reader, with a made-up headline example for each so I can see the difference, (2) who first argued that this is ideological, when, and what the actual newspaper example they used was (if you know it), (3) whether it's true that the passive ALWAYS hides who did something, because my dad says that's nonsense and that there are perfectly normal reasons to use it, and (4) which of these ideas are generally agreed and which are just one school of linguists' opinion, because I want to put real names and dates in the essay and not just write "linguists say". Please say if you aren't sure about a name or a date rather than guessing, I'd rather check it myself. Don't write any of the essay for me, I just need the background sorted.
strong_answer_must: Define the agentless passive precisely: a passive clause with no 'by' phrase, so the agent is not stated (e.g. an invented headline such as 'Protesters injured in city centre'); contrast it with a passive that keeps the agent in a by-phrase and with the active version that names the agent first.

Define nominalisation as turning a process (verb) into a noun ('police shot protesters' becomes 'the shooting'), which lets the writer drop the participants and the tense; give an invented headline example and explain that the two devices are different things that are often used together.

Attribute the 'ideological' argument to critical linguistics: Roger Fowler, Bob Hodge, Gunther Kress and Tony Trew, Language and Control (1979), and specifically Tony Trew's analysis of how British newspapers reported the shooting of demonstrators by police in Salisbury, Rhodesia, in June 1975: one paper's headline put the demonstrators first as 'rioting' and the police in an agentless or by-phrase position, another's used an active clause with the police as the agent; later reports nominalised the event so the agent vanished. Exact headline wording may be described rather than quoted, and if quoted should be flagged as needing verification against Trew's chapter.

Attribute the grammatical toolkit (transitivity: process, participants, circumstances) to M. A. K. Halliday's systemic functional grammar (An Introduction to Functional Grammar, 1985, with earlier work in the 1970s) and the later, broader movement to Norman Fairclough, Language and Power (1989), and critical discourse analysis; mark any further names as uncertain if the answer is unsure.

Answer (3) correctly: the passive does not always hide the agent; only the agentless passive omits it, and agentless passives are normal when the agent is unknown, obvious, or irrelevant, or when the affected participant is the topic (given information first). So a single passive proves nothing; the argument depends on patterns across a text and on comparing the choice with available alternatives.

Distinguish what is generally agreed (the grammar: how passives and nominalisations work; that they can omit agency; that headlines foreground whatever comes first) from what is contested (that such choices are necessarily ideological or intentional). Name a dissenting position, for example Geoffrey Pullum's argument that condemnation of the passive is overdone and that George Orwell's 1946 essay 'Politics and the English Language' attacks the passive while using it; label it as a counter-position with attribution.
Be honest about uncertainty: say which names, dates and headline wordings the student should verify in a library copy or school database, rather than presenting everything with equal confidence.

Give the student a method for the HL essay without writing it: compare headline and first paragraph of two reports of the same event, tabulate who is the grammatical agent, count agentless passives and nominalisations, and link the pattern to each paper's audience; treat the HL essay's rules (word limit, choice of text) as something to confirm with the teacher or the current IB guide rather than asserting them.
End with one tagged Sources line; the theorists must be tagged 'recalled, not consulted' (nothing was retrieved), and no URLs anywhere.
pitfalls: Misattribution: crediting the 1975 headline study to Fairclough, Halliday, Chomsky or Orwell; giving Language and Control as 1989 or Language and Power as 1979; calling Fowler et al. 'critical discourse analysis' (that label came later, with Fairclough).

Fabrication: inventing a different newspaper, country or year for the example, inventing exact headline wording with full confidence, inventing a 'study' with a percentage ('70% of headlines use the passive'), or quoting Orwell, Fairclough or Trew verbatim from memory.

Grammar errors: treating every passive as agent-hiding; counting 'there were deaths' or 'the protest turned violent' as passives; conflating nominalisation with the passive; calling an adjective ('the injured') a passive.

A leap from 'the passive can hide agency' to 'the newspaper intended to protect the police' without saying this is an interpretation that needs the comparison with the other paper and the rest of the text.
Answering (4) with 'linguists agree' or 'most scholars think' without naming who, or presenting the ideological reading as settled fact.

Writing the essay: supplying a thesis statement, a paragraph, or a 'you could write...' passage the student could paste; or stating HL essay requirements (word count, text choice) as fact without a hedge.
Format failures: a missing or untagged Sources line, a URL, or revealing any internal code.
